problem: Learning-based outdoor navigation (ViNT, NoMaD, GNM, CityWalker) is short-range, needs environment-specific data and copes poorly with dynamic objects. Scene-graph/LLM navigation methods are mostly indoor and static, so long-range language-goal navigation in dynamic outdoor scenes is not handled.
motivation: Real outdoor robots must accept abstract, open-vocabulary goals (e.g., a building or object) from arbitrary start points over hundreds of meters, while pedestrians and vehicles keep changing the scene. Fusing offline map data with real-time perception in a hierarchical, continuously updated graph lets an LLM do RAG-style retrieval without hallucination, and dynamic objects can be filtered out of both the graph and the local map.
key_idea: Build an LLM-clustered multi-level Embodied Graph (buildings from offline maps plus tracked object nodes, with dynamic objects filtered by spatial-temporal corridors) used as a RAG knowledge base for goal retrieval, followed by global route planning and local NMPC-CBF planning on a dynamic-object-free map.
insight: The online-updated graph is what matters: disabling Embodied Graph updates drops SR from 90 to 78 and SPL from 80.1 to 54.7 (Table 3). Hierarchical retrieval makes small local LLMs (12-14B) nearly as good as GPT-4o (SR 82-85 vs 88), so edge deployment is feasible. Explicit dynamic-obstacle handling (RH-Map plus CBF) gives far fewer collisions than end-to-end CityWalker with comparable SR.
method: Open-vocabulary tracking: YOLO-World plus ByteTrack give 2D masks. LiDAR points projected into the masks give 3D boxes and centroids, which are placed in the world frame using FAST-LIO2 odometry and inserted or updated as object nodes.
Ego-trajectory nodes: ego position/velocity nodes are added whenever movement exceeds a threshold d, linked by edges, and later reused for Dijkstra global planning over previously visited places.

Spatial-temporal corridor filter: CenterPoint plus LIOsegmot classify objects as dynamic/static/quasi-static; an object's trajectory of boxes over time forms a corridor, and objects that exceed a displacement threshold of k steps are removed from the graph.

Hierarchical Embodied Graph: building nodes from offline maps sit at the top level L and object nodes at L-1. Bottom-up clustering uses a similarity mixing haversine spatial kernel and embedding cosine similarity (weight alpha), and an LLM summarizes each cluster.

Hierarchical RAG retrieval: an LLM scores nodes level by level (softmax with sharpness gamma) and path scores are multiplied. Candidates are re-ranked with a spatial-proximity term to the current location (weight beta) to pick the goal.

Global planning: if the goal is not reachable from the past trajectory, a coarse route comes from offline road maps or Google Maps/Amap APIs; otherwise Dijkstra on the trajectory graph gives waypoints.

Local planning: RH-Map (region-wise hash map) removes dynamic obstacle trails, informed-RRT* plus B-spline give the reference path, and NMPC with a control barrier function tracks it around predicted pedestrians and vehicles.

setting.backbone: YOLO-World + ByteTrack + CenterPoint (pretrained), LLM for graph summarization/retrieval (Deepseek-R1-Distill-14B, Qwen3-14B, phi4-14B, Gemma3-12B, or GPT-4o), NMPC-CBF planner
setting.observation: RGB (RealSense D435i) + 3D LiDAR + IMU + RTK GNSS/INS, plus offline map data
setting.action_space: continuous velocity control (v, omega) from NMPC-CBF along a planned trajectory
setting.simulator: Gazebo (urban environment with pedestrians and vehicles)
setting.privileged: offline map data (building/road maps); initial graph built by full-environment exploration in simulation; Google Maps/Amap routes

numbers_note: Custom Gazebo benchmark, no standard benchmark. Table 1 does not state which LLM was used. Real-world results are qualitative (130 m and 512 m trials); parameter ablation only in a figure.
results: In simulation CausalNav matches or beats all baselines on SR/SPL with far fewer collisions (Large: SR 80 equal to CityWalker, CC 1.2 vs 4.5; Medium SR 92 vs CityWalker 85). In the real world it is the only method to finish the 512 m building-level task, and it runs at about 105 ms per cycle.
limitations: Scalability, robustness to extreme lighting/weather and long-horizon consistency remain open issues
Evaluation is on a small custom Gazebo setup (25 tasks) with a few real-world trials, and no standard VLN benchmark
Relies on offline maps, LiDAR/GNSS localization and an initial exploration to build the graph
